title: U.S. Department of Commerce, Bureau of Industry and Security: Applicability of the Congressional Review Act to the Rescission of the Artificial Intelligence Diffusion Rule (B-337935)
key_claim: GAO concluded that Commerce's press release announcing non-enforcement of the AI Diffusion Rule is itself a rule under the Administrative Procedure Act, subject to Congressional Review Act submission requirements, while the underlying rule remains in the Code of Federal Regulations.
frame_summary: GAO argues that a blanket non-enforcement announcement is not internal housekeeping but a rule that substantively alters regulated parties' obligations, and therefore must be submitted to Congress and the Comptroller General before it can take effect.
verbatim_quote: We conclude that the Press Release meets the APA definition of a rule and that no CRA exception applies. Therefore, the Press Release is a rule subject to CRA's submission requirements.
verbatim_list: Because Commerce is operating as if the rule were already rescinded by applying a categorical non-enforcement policy, our analysis focuses on whether the agency's announced non‑enforcement policy constitutes a rule under CRA.
Commerce further explained that until the rulemaking process is complete, the AI Diffusion Framework remains in the Code of Federal Regulations.
notes: Decision requested by Senator Elizabeth Warren (letter of 19 November 2025); Commerce responded 30 January 2026. title: Deletion of Obsolete Regulations (seventh Direct Final Rule, GN Docket No. 25-133)
key_claim: The FCC's seventh direct final rule repeals rule provisions without prior notice and comment under the good-cause standard, taking effect automatically unless significant adverse comment is filed within a short window.
frame_summary: The Commission argues that repealing obsolete provisions is a case where notice and comment is legally unnecessary, and that the direct final rule process voluntarily restores a narrow comment opportunity the good-cause standard does not require.
verbatim_quote: With this seventh *Direct Final Rule,* the Commission will have eliminated approximately 1,274 rule provisions, 149,566 words, and more than 338 pages from the Code of Federal Regulation.
verbatim_list: effective August 21, 2026 without further action, unless adverse comment is received by July 13, 2026. If adverse comment is received, the Commission will publish a timely withdrawal of the rule in the Federal Register.
By proceeding through a direct final rule, we choose to provide expanded opportunities for public comment even though the “good cause” standard does not legally require us to do so

title: Anticipatory Deregulation and the Endangerment Rescission
date_evidence:
[Administrative Law] [Blog Essay] March 13, 2026

# Anticipatory Deregulation and the Endangerment Rescission
key_claim: Agencies are repealing rules on the ground that the rules were unlawful from the outset, a strategy intended to bar successors from reinstating them, and one that the presidential memorandum pairs with the APA good-cause exception.
frame_summary: The essay argues that anticipatory deregulation is a policy-entrenchment strategy that seeks to convert contestable legal judgements into binding constraints on future administrations, and that it is vulnerable under Regents because reliance interests must still be considered.
verbatim_quote: the Administration seeks to repeal regulations not on the grounds that conditions have shifted or priorities changed but that the rule is illegal and was promulgated ultra vires.
verbatim_list: If successful, the maneuver will not merely repeal the determination but illegalize it, barring any future administration from replacing it.
Even if the administration were duty-bound to root out illegal regulations, illegality provides no procedural escape hatch.

title: Diary of deconstruction: White House releases 2026 Unified Agenda of Federal Regulations
date_evidence: [Clyde Wayne Crews] • 07/06/2026 (US format, 6 July 2026); page metadata: meta-article:modified_time: 2026-07-06T15:33:41+00:00
key_claim: The 2026 Unified Agenda carries 3,954 entries, the highest count since 2012, because rescissions and withdrawals themselves generate rulemaking entries; final rules published stand at 1,519.
frame_summary: CEI argues that a deregulatory programme paradoxically inflates the rulemaking pipeline, since undoing a rule usually requires writing one, and that headline rule counts therefore say little about how much regulation firms actually face.
verbatim_quote: The 3,954 entries in the new edition, curiously enough, represent the highest count since 2012.
verbatim_list: There have been only 1,519 final rules published so far in the Federal Register, meaning the administration remains on track for another of the lowest annual rule counts on record.
A rule cannot simply be eliminated in pursuit of deregulation; under the Administrative Procedure Act, a replacement rule typically must be drafted.
The active rule count of 2,518 is up from 2,098 in last year's edition.

title: Trump's Swift Deregulation Strategy Falls Flat With Agencies
key_claim: A Bloomberg Law analysis found that of roughly 2,800 rules published since the mandated review period closed, only two agencies beyond the Energy Department invoked the good cause exception on the basis of the ten Supreme Court cases the White House identified.
frame_summary: Bloomberg Law argues that agencies have quietly declined the fast-track repeal strategy because they doubt its legal defensibility, and that the administration has instead achieved its effects through enforcement shifts and staffing cuts that are easier for successors to reverse.
verbatim_quote: While the administration has published about 2,800 rules since the close of the mandated regulatory review period, only two other agencies have used the good cause exception based on one of the cases that the White House highlighted.
verbatim_list: Just because a rule is still on the books, it doesn't mean much if nobody is willing to enforce the rule or nobody is in office to enforce the rule,

The administration has made major changes to defang the regulatory state, including shifting enforcement priorities and slashing agency personnel, although some of those moves might be easier for future administrations to reverse compared to ditching rules.
Agencies have cited Trump's quickie deregulation policy in eight other withdrawals since last April, with varied justifications for why the measure at issue was unlawful.

title: Client Alert: 2026 Mid-Year Update on DOJ Corporate and White Collar Enforcement
key_claim: Counsel advise that the taper in FCPA enforcement is a re-prioritisation rather than a repeal, that limitations periods outlast an administration, and that companies should not roll back compliance controls in response.
frame_summary: The alert argues that enforcement-posture changes are the wrong basis for compliance decisions, because the underlying legal exposure survives the posture and whistleblower and qui tam channels operate regardless of agency appetite.
verbatim_quote: Limitations periods outlast any administration, so significant compliance rollbacks remain risky.
verbatim_list: Do not roll back compliance: The taper of FCPA enforcement is not a repeal, and limitations periods outlast administrations.
Combined with FCA qui tam incentives in the trade context, the practical result is that the window to self-disclose ahead of a whistleblower is narrowing.
